    Get started

    quickmap.Rmd

    QuickMap makes air quality maps from the data you already have — a diffusion tube file, a sensor-network export, or a live data source such as an OpenAir data pull. Maps are self-contained files, so you can email them or put them on a website, and compact, fast animations are easy to create.

    This page works through two builds. Part 1 grows one report map, a step at a time, from a single line of code; Part 2 grows an animated pollution episode. The maps shown are real QuickMap output — click, drag and play with them. Along the way, each step points to the chapter that takes that feature further.

    1. Install

    Install from GitHub:

    # install.packages("devtools")            # if you don't have it
devtools::install_github("ngnrfsk/quickmap")

    While the repository is private, install_github() needs a GitHub personal access token: create one at github.com → Settings → Developer settings, then run Sys.setenv(GITHUB_PAT = "your-token") first. This step disappears when the package is released.

    Part 1 — Build a report map

    One dataset (a Wandsworth diffusion tube survey), one map, growing by one line per step.

    2. Make your first map — one argument 

    library(quickmap)                           # load the quickmap library
quickmap(
  "~/my_data/tubes_wandsworth.csv"  # diffusion tube data
)

    One input — the measurement data — is all quickmap() needs. The data here is an ordinary diffusion tube spreadsheet saved as CSV:

    Easting Northing 2017 2018 … 2024 Label
    528900 172431 33 31 … 15.9 11b Elmbourne Road
    530129 177727 49 … 22.9 1 Nine Elms

    Minimum required: Easting, Northing and at least one year column. Anything else is optional. (Full input specifications: the Your data chapter.)

    QuickMap converts the coordinates, colours each site by the WHO NO2 bands, fits the view to the data, and writes aq_maps/quickmap.html — a single self-contained file. Open it in any browser, attach it to an email, or put it on a website (it does need an internet connection to download the background map). Here is that exact file:

    Reading the map:

    • Symbols are monitoring sites, coloured by pollution level — green is good, red is bad. Labels can be added that appear on hover — step 8.
    • The legend (along the bottom) names each colour band. The bands come from a colour scale (who_no2 by default) — swap it with colour_scale =, as Part 2 does. Click the legend header to collapse it.
    • The time slider (bottom of the map) appears because your CSV had several year columns. Drag it, step with ‹ ›, or press play to animate.
    • The banner (top) is the map’s title — customised in step 7.

    3. Draw a borough boundary

    Air quality reporting is usually about a place; naming it draws its boundary and frames the map around it:

    quickmap(
  "~/my_data/tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs = "Wandsworth"                   # NEW: the boundary to draw
)

    More on boundaries:

    • boroughs takes one name, several (c("Wandsworth", "Richmond")), or "All" for every London borough.
    • The area’s name can be written on the map with boundary_labels = TRUE — useful on multi-borough maps.
    • The boundary also drives the next step’s vignette and the map’s framing.

    4. The vignette — focus attention inside the boundary

    The map above dims everything outside Wandsworth. That is the vignette, on by default whenever a boundary is drawn, so the reader’s eye goes to the area the map is about. Written out explicitly:

    quickmap(
  "~/my_data/tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs = "Wandsworth",
  vignette = TRUE                           # NEW: dim outside the boundary
)                                           #      (the default with a boundary)

    Set vignette = FALSE to show the surroundings at full brightness:

    The vignette’s colour follows the map’s theme — themes bundle all such choices into one reusable YAML file (?load_theme).

    5. Save typing: tell QuickMap where your data lives

    Optional, but worth doing once: if your data files sit in one folder, set DATA_PATH and use bare filenames everywhere (the rest of this page assumes it is set):

    Sys.setenv(
  DATA_PATH = "~/my_data"                  # folder where your data lives
)
quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",          # NEW: just the filename
  boroughs = "Wandsworth"
)

    6. Export a static map for a report

    Documents need still images. export_image writes a JPG next to the HTML, at any size — text and legend scale with the image:

    library(quickmap)                          # (already loaded if you followed above)
quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs      = "Wandsworth",
  display_times = "2024",                  # NEW: one year -> one image
  export_image  = c(1200, 900)             # NEW: JPG width x height, pixels
)
    The exported JPG: 1200×900, ready for a report

    With several time steps selected you get one JPG per step; export_image = TRUE uses the default 1200×1200. display_times also subsets interactive maps — pick any years, months or hours present in the data.

    7. Add a title and choose the file name

    Maps usually need a title for the banner, and a file name you’ll recognise later:

    quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs    = "Wandsworth",
  title       = "Wandsworth NO2, 2017-2024", # NEW: banner text
  output_file = "wandsworth_no2.html"        # NEW: file written to aq_maps/
)

    The accent colour under the title can be set directly with banner_colour =; the banner’s style (white strip or colour bar) and the full colour scheme are theme settings (?load_theme).

    8. Add labels to the symbols

    Readers often want the number behind a colour. marker_labels = TRUE shows each site’s value when you hover over its symbol — try it on the map below:

    quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs      = "Wandsworth",
  title         = "Wandsworth NO2, 2017-2024",
  marker_labels = TRUE                       # NEW: values appear on hover
)

    Labels have five modes — off, values on hover, values always shown, and site names (from a Label or School column) on hover or always shown: marker_labels = "values_on", "labels", "labels_on" (?quickmap).

    9. Combine several measurement networks

    Different monitoring networks — and context like schools — go on one map by listing the files. Each network keeps its own symbol, and putting the symbols in the title turns the banner into a key:

    quickmap(
  list(
    "tubes_merton.csv",                             # diffusion tubes
    "sensors_london.RData", # sensor network
    "schools_merton.csv"                                   # school locations
  ),
  boroughs = "Merton",
  title = "Merton NO2: ● tubes ◆ sensors ✖ schools" # NEW: symbols as a key
)

    Naming layers, choosing each network’s pollutant or symbol (data_symbols, qm_layer()), and mapping data frames you built yourself: the Layers chapter — start at “Use the layers list to add sources”.

    Part 2 — Build an animation

    A new dataset (five days of hourly sensor readings during a January 2024 pollution episode), and two steps. These maps keep the default OpenStreetMap background; for dense data a paler background can suit better — switching is one theme line (map: base_tiles: "CartoDB.Positron", ?load_theme).

    10. Animate a pollution episode

    This maps 108 hourly time steps and starts playing by itself — pause it with the round button, drag the slider to any hour, or change the pace with the multiplier button at the right of the card:

    quickmap(
  from_rdata("episode_london.RData", # hourly sensor export
             "pm25",                              # pollutant to map
             name = "Sensors"),                   # layer name for the map
  boroughs     = c("Wandsworth", "Richmond"),     # two boundaries
  colour_scale = "stripes_pm25",                  # a PM2.5 colour scale
  title        = "PM2.5 Episode: Jan 15-20, 2024",
  output_file  = "episode.html",
  autoplay     = TRUE,                            # play on open
  play_speed   = 500                              # ms per hour; omit to
)                                                 # let the step count decide

    Above 50 time steps QuickMap automatically switches to a compact storage format, so even this five-day hourly animation stays around 1 MB — small enough to email. Colour scales for other pollutants and boroughs: ?load_colour_scale.

    11. Add live wind to the animation

    Where did the pollution come from? An animated wind-particle overlay answers that at a glance. from_worldmet() fetches real weather-station data (here Heathrow) from NOAA, and the particles advance with the time slider:

    heathrow <- from_worldmet(station = "037720-99999", # Heathrow station id
                          year = 2024)              # fetches from NOAA
quickmap(
  from_rdata("episode_london.RData", "pm25", name = "Sensors"),
  boroughs     = c("Wandsworth", "Richmond"),
  colour_scale = "stripes_pm25",
  title        = "PM2.5 Episode with wind: Jan 15-20, 2024",
  output_file  = "episode_wind.html",
  autoplay     = TRUE,
  play_speed   = 500,
  wind         = heathrow                           # NEW: the wind overlay
)

    Wind particles are coloured by wind speed. Requires the worldmet package and an internet connection for the NOAA fetch; particle styling and station choice: the Wind chapter.

    Where next

    • Function help — ?quickmap lists every parameter.
